newsitem.title: UK: British Conservative defects to opposition party.
newsitem.headline: British Conservative defects to opposition party.

text.p: A member of Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives defected on Saturday to the opposition Liberal Democrats, denting the optimism with which the ruling party had ended its annual conference a day earlier.

The defection by Peter Thurnham will not affect Major's parliamentary majority of just two, because the maverick politician resigned from the party whip in February which meant he was not expected to vote with the government.
"I can no longer support a government which has so lost touch with the basic values of decency that they have forfeited the trust and respect of the British people," Thurnham said.

In a lengthy statement, Thurnham outlined his "despair" over Major's weak leadership, party disunity, education policy and calls by his colleagues for vote-winning tax cuts before the next general election.
"I cannot, above all, accept the latest attempts by the Government to suppress enquiries into allegations of sleaze which poison the very basis of our democracy," Thurnham said.

Thurnham's defection came the day after the Conservatives ended a triumphant annual conference at which party splits were hidden and Major won plaudits for an informal question and answer session as well as his set-piece speech.

Before the party conference, held in Bournemouth, southern England, Major had been mired in allegations that some members of his party had taken bribes to ask questions in parliament and others had tried to stifle an inquiry into the matter.
Thurnham resigned from the party whip over another inquiry, which severely criticised government ministers for their part in the sales of arms to Iraq in the late 1980s.
The member of parliament for the constituency of Bolton North East in northern England had previously said he was considering leaving the ruling party.
His defection is likely to cause the Conservatives less grief than the loss the week before the conference of Lord McAlpine, a former party treasurer and deputy chairman.
McAlpine left to join the newly-formed Referendum Party of tycoon Sir James Goldsmith.
A spokeswoman for the Conservatives said the party was unperturbed by the loss of Thurnham.
"This doesn't change anything. Our majority is still the same, which is two," she said.
Major's majority rose from just one last week, following the death of a Labour member of parliament.
Nevertheless, Thurnham is the latest in a stream of Conservative MP's who have defected or been forced to resign following sleaze allegations, damaging the ruling party's image.
On the eve of last year's party conference, Conservative MP Alan Howard, went over to opposition Labour Party. Another, Emma Nicholson, defected to the Liberal Democrats in December.
Earlier on Saturday, the small anti-European Independence Party claimed yet another Conservative MP was about to defect and become its leader.
With only seven months left until Major must call a general election, his party is trailing Labour by 20 points in opinion polls.
Labour leader Tony Blair, on a trip to South Africa, described Thurnham's move as "great news."
"It shows that even life-long Conservatives are deserting the party," he told reporters in Johannesburg.
